binders: x is the one-dimensional spatial coordinate and t is time; the initial slice is t = 0 [printed page 1, introduction to (1.1); printed page 5, (1.11)].

q is the unknown state depending on x and t; the introductory system permits vector states in ℝ^m, with the scalar case m = 1 also discussed [printed page 1, paragraph following (1.1) and scalar-case paragraph].
q_l and q_r are the constant left and right initial states [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening paragraph and (1.11)].
The initial jump is at a spatial point represented as x = 0; “say x = 0” presents the location as a choice [printed page 5, sentence introducing (1.11)].
hypotheses: The governing equation is hyperbolic [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, “the hyperbolic equation together with special initial data”].
The initial data are piecewise constant with a single jump discontinuity, represented at x = 0 [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, sentence preceding (1.11)].
conclusions: A hyperbolic equation together with the specified two-state initial data is the problem called a Riemann problem [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening paragraph].
The initial condition requires q(x,0) = q_l for every x < 0 and q(x,0) = q_r for every x > 0; (1.11) imposes no displayed value at x = 0 [printed page 5, (1.11), two strict-inequality branches].
definitions_and_conventions: The equation is part of the problem being defined; the two-state initial profile alone does not exhaust the definition [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, “equation together with special initial data”].
For the constant-coefficient linear system (1.1), hyperbolicity means real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors of A [printed page 3, opening paragraph].
The symbols q_l and q_r designate left and right states by the conditions x < 0 and x > 0, respectively [printed page 5, (1.11)].
implicit_context: The chapter introduces time-dependent problems and one-space-dimensional systems; (1.11) uses that spatial and temporal notation [printed page 1, paragraph introducing (1.1); printed page 5, (1.11)].

Discontinuous conservation-law solutions need not satisfy the differential equation classically at the discontinuity; the source instead identifies the integral conservation law as fundamental there [printed page 5, paragraph beginning “At a discontinuity in q”].

Conservation laws are an important class in the chapter, but the Riemann-problem definition says “hyperbolic equation”; the later discussion explicitly includes equations outside conservation form [printed page 3, Section 1.1; printed page 5, Section 1.2.1; printed page 8, second paragraph].

details: Each branch in (1.11) applies throughout its indicated open spatial half-line at initial time; the display does not constrain q at positive times [printed page 5, (1.11)].
Neither equality with q_l nor equality with q_r is specified at x = 0 [printed page 5, (1.11), strict inequalities].
The definition specifies an equation and initial data; it does not explicitly assert existence or uniqueness of a solution [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening paragraph and (1.11)].
The subsequent similarity and finite-wave description is qualified by “typically”; it is not stated as an unconditional requirement in the definition [printed page 5, paragraph after (1.11)].

For neighboring grid-cell averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i, the source chooses q_l = Q_{i−1} and q_r = Q_i to obtain information for flux computation and a cell-average update [printed page 5, paragraph after (1.11)].

This neighboring-cell construction is an application following the definition, rather than a prerequisite that every Riemann problem originate from a grid [printed page 5, opening definition followed by the conditional sentence beginning “If Q_{i−1} and Q_i”].

undebatable_constraints: Preserve the governing hyperbolic equation as a constituent of the Riemann problem [printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, opening sentence].
Preserve the initial time t = 0, constant left and right states, and the strict spatial inequalities in (1.11) [printed page 5, (1.11)].
Do not attribute a prescribed interface value to the source: neither displayed branch includes x = 0 [printed page 5, (1.11)].
Do not turn the typical similarity and finite-wave description into an unconditional theorem or defining hypothesis [printed page 5, paragraph after (1.11), “typically”].
Do not require classical differential satisfaction at a discontinuity on the authority of this passage [printed page 5, paragraph beginning “At a discontinuity in q”].

ambiguities.issue: Whether equal left and right states are included as a degenerate Riemann problem.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, calls the data a “single jump discontinuity,” but (1.11) does not explicitly state q_l ≠ q_r.
ambiguities.impact: The prose describes a genuine jump, while the displayed equations alone allow equal states. The source does not explicitly settle inclusion of the degenerate case.

ambiguities.issue: The initial value at the interface.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed page 5, (1.11), specifies only x < 0 and x > 0.
ambiguities.impact: Choosing a value at x = 0 requires an additional convention. The passage does not explicitly explain whether or in what solution sense that choice is immaterial.

ambiguities.issue: The precise solution concept and general admissibility conditions.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed page 5, Section 1.2.1, defines the problem without specifying a solution space or admissibility criterion; the preceding discussion says classical differential satisfaction fails at discontinuities.
ambiguities.impact: A particular weak-solution definition, entropy condition, regularity requirement, or existence-and-uniqueness assertion cannot be recovered from the selected definition alone.

contract_plain_english: Section 1.2.1 defines a Riemann problem as a hyperbolic equation supplied with initial data consisting of two constant states separated at a point, written as x = 0: q(x,0) = q_l for x < 0 and q(x,0) = q_r for x > 0 [printed page 5, opening paragraph and (1.11)]. The interface value is unspecified, and the prose's genuine-jump wording leaves the equal-state case unresolved by the display. The subsequent similarity and finite-wave description is expressly typical, rather than an unconditional assertion [printed page 5, paragraph after (1.11)].
